subject: research/mimic-anycontext-size
professional: an NLP researcher who works on LLM-as-zero-shot-detector evaluation and scaling behaviour (zero-shot machine-text detection, RAID/MAGE-style benchmarks, prompted-classifier calibration): first checks that scores are scored the way the README says, that the AUROC differences are larger than the sampling error of 30+30 texts, that a size trend is not read off two points and a prompt chosen on the test set, and whether the 'inverted' detector is a real property of the model or an artefact of the Yes/No probe

evidence.correctness: No model was run (none needed: the per-text logit differences are cached in scores_*.json). I recomputed with my own script (scratchpad rc.py: a brute-force pairwise P(human>machine) with ties counted half, written without importing core.py or anyprompt.py) from the shipped scores_Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct.json and scores_Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.json, 64 keys of 30 scores each per model. (1) Mean AUROC by candidate: 0.5B [0.2775, 0.2765, 0.2890, 0.2957], 1.5B [0.3292, 0.3004, 0.3715, 0.3890], identical to results.json to 15 digits. (2) Plain-prompt per-family values: 1.5B news 0.5044, books 0.1444, poetry 0.1556, recipes 0.3578; 0.5B recipes 0.0878, poetry 0.2411, all match results.json and the README's prose ('recipes 0.09 to 0.36, news 0.31 to 0.50, books 0.29 to 0.14, poetry 0.24 to 0.16'). (3) Cells below 0.5: 32 of 32 (0.5B) and 27 of 32 (1.5B), the README table and the 0.84375 in results.json; sign-flipped plain 0.7225 and 0.6708. (4) Pooled AUROC by candidate also matches. (5) Prompt spread 0.019 (0.5B) and 0.089 (1.5B) matches 'the spread ... is 0.09 against 0.02'. (6) README says 0.5B plain 0.278 equals the earlier project: mimic-anycontext-prompt/README.md line 17 gives 0.278. (7) The README's standard error of about 0.06: Hanley-McNeil for A=0.3, n=30+30 gives about 0.067, consistent. Verified left padding (mimic-loop/lm.py:10) so the last-token logit read in logit_diff is the right position. Limit: I did not rerun the models, so whether the cached scores are what Qwen outputs was not checked; the scores' provenance rests on the author's run.
evidence.completeness: Claimed and checked: 4 unit tests (ran, 4 pass); results table (reproduces); both 0.5B and 1.5B scored with all four candidates on all eight families (64 keys each, all present); results.json and experiments/figure.svg present; project.json present; live-page URL declared. Not delivered: the 3B model. sizerun.py lists it in MODELS, the tests assert three models and three cache paths, and figure.py allocates three colours, but no scores_Qwen2.5-3B file or results.json entry exists; the README states this openly, so it is honest, but the question 'does a bigger model cross 0.5' is therefore answered only with two points, and the project's own 'Next steps' list the missing 3B and a non-Qwen family. The docs/posts directory has no post for this project (grep for 'size' and 'inversion' found none about it). The reproduce block says 'python3 -m unittest' needs no model: true (ran with a bare python3, no numpy needed). I did not run sizerun.py itself because it downloads models.
evidence.verification: Ran `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` in research/mimic-anycontext-size: 4 tests, 4 pass. They assert the MODELS list order, that three cache paths differ, that the first four candidates are a prefix of the sibling project's list, and that core.auroc is right on two toy cases. None calls analyse() or run(). Mutation: in sizerun.py analyse() I changed `"flipped_plain_mean": 1 - per[0]` to `per[0]` and `< 0.5` to `> 0.5` in the below-half share (two seeded bugs, one edit); all 4 tests still passed (both mutations survived). Reverted with git checkout; git status for the project is clean. analyse() is the whole of the reported result and it is untested, and nothing asserts that results.json equals a rerun on the committed score caches, although that check is a three-line test with no model needed.
evidence.craft: Read sizerun.py (59 lines), figure.py (25), tests/test_sizerun.py (23), and the sibling anyprompt.py and mimic-loop lm.py/core.py that it relies on. Small, resumable (per-candidate cache dump) and it reuses the sibling project's loader instead of copying it, which is good. Defects: (a) analyse() writes results.json as a side effect and silently skips a model with no cache, so the 3B model is dropped without a warning; (b) figure.py hard-codes three colours and a y-axis cap of 0.6 (a family at AUROC above 0.6 would be clipped silently); (c) the cache is dumped only after a whole candidate, so a crash during the 2-hour 1.5B pass loses up to a candidate, which for 1.5B is about 30 minutes; (d) sys.path insertion and the `import lm` inside run() make the module import order-sensitive; (e) logit_diff runs a plain forward on left-padded batches without position_ids, so scores depend slightly on batch composition (not tested, probably small); (f) the Yes and No token ids are the first sub-token of 'Yes'/'No' with no check that the model's first answer token is one of them. No unhandled-input bug hit in the paths run.
evidence.claims: Each README claim against a file: all table numbers, the per-family movements, '27 of 32', '0.504 for news', 'sign flipped 0.722/0.671', 'spread 0.09 vs 0.02' reproduce from the score caches (see correctness). 'The 0.5B numbers match the earlier project' is backed by mimic-anycontext-prompt/README.md line 17. Limits are stated and accurate: two sizes of one family, four prompts, 'best of 4 chosen on test texts, optimistic', standard error about 0.06, one seed, plain-prompt RAID text, produced with AI assistance, no lab affiliation. Weaker points: (1) the lede 'does a bigger Qwen make a better detector? Partly' and 'Bigger helps on average' rest on a plain-prompt gain of +0.05 (0.278 to 0.329) whose uncertainty the README does not give: the family SE is 0.06 and the mean over eight families is about 0.02 if independent, so the gain is around two standard errors, which is suggestive, not established, and 'prompts matter more at 1.5B' compares a 0.09 spread against a 0.02 spread with four hand-picked-by-seed prompts and no interval; the README does hedge this ('read this as prompt choice starts to matter, not a ranking'). (2) Limitations say size 'is confounded with nothing else' which is not strictly true: the 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 instruct models also differ in training mix and chat tuning depth, and the 400-character cut interacts with tokeniser vocabulary identical across both, so the claim is acceptable but overstated. (3) 'Track 11' and the live page are asserted; I did not load the live page.
evidence.fitness: The job: a researcher asked in the sibling project whether a 0.5B model's below-chance detector is a size effect. They get a direct, cheap answer for two sizes, the cached scores so they can re-score offline, and an explicit statement that 3B was not run. They can build on it only as a data point: no text-level bootstrap or paired test for the 0.5B-to-1.5B change on the same 480 texts (a paired bootstrap is trivial with the shipped scores), only four prompts, and a probe whose inversion is unexplained (is the model answering Yes to fluent machine text? Is it a position/format bias on 'Yes'? A calibration-free control such as comparing mean logit to a permuted-label null, or a log-probability based Binoculars/perplexity score on the same texts, is not provided). Without 3B or a second family there is no trend. The sign-flip result (0.72/0.67) is flagged as a curiosity that would need labelled calibration data, which is correct.
evidence.domain: Nearest prior work: zero-shot LLM-as-detector results (Mitchell et al. 2023, DetectGPT; Hans et al. 2024, Binoculars) which show that raw LLM judgement of 'was this written by an AI' is poor and often biased toward calling machine text human, and RAID (Dugan et al. 2024), the data source, which reports that off-the-shelf detectors vary with domain; and the prompted-classifier literature on inverted or biased zero-shot ratings (e.g. Zhao et al. 2021 calibrate-before-use). The project cites RAID only for data; it does not cite Binoculars/DetectGPT or calibrate-before-use, which a reviewer would expect for a below-chance zero-shot score. As a result the finding (inversion shrinks but persists from 0.5B to 1.5B for a Yes/No probe) is consistent with that literature but not clearly new, and with two sizes it cannot support a scaling claim. Soundness: the method is right for what it claims (fixed prompts, same texts, held-out of any selection, paired design implicit), AUROC is the usual headline but there is no TPR at fixed FPR, no CI, no calibration of the Yes/No offset, and a 'best of 4' reported next to fixed prompts. A senior researcher would call it a sound pilot note, not a result.

defects.what: The tests do not touch analyse(), the function that produces every reported number. Two seeded bugs (flipped_plain_mean = per[0] instead of 1 - per[0], and the below-0.5 share inverted to > 0.5) both left all 4 tests green. A model-free test that runs analyse() on the committed scores_*.json and compares with results.json would catch both.

The headline 'bigger helps on average' (+0.05 plain AUROC, +0.09 best-of-4) has no uncertainty on the difference and the 'best of 4' is chosen on the test texts; a paired bootstrap over the 480 shared texts is possible from the shipped scores but not done. Two model sizes cannot show a trend, and the 3B arm is listed in MODELS and the tests but never ran (README discloses).

No explanation of the inversion and no control for the probe: no comparison with a perplexity or Binoculars-style score on the same texts, no calibration of the Yes/No offset, and prior work on zero-shot LLM judges and calibration is not cited, so novelty is unclear.

analyse() silently skips a model whose cache is missing (3B dropped without warning), figure.py clips any AUROC above 0.6 and assumes three models at most, the cache is saved per candidate not per family, and the left-padded forward pass passes no position_ids. 'Size is confounded with nothing else' is slightly overstated (training mix differs between 0.5B and 1.5B).

verdict: Honest, small and correct: every number I recomputed from the cached scores with an independent AUROC (all 8 plain-prompt family values for both models, the four candidate means, 27 of 32 and 32 of 32 cells below chance, the flipped means, the prompt spreads) matches results.json and the README to many digits, the limits are stated, and the missing 3B arm is disclosed. It does not meet the bar because verification is a 1: four toy tests never call analyse(), and two seeded bugs in it survived. It is also unfinished against its own plan (the 3B model is listed but not run), carries no uncertainty on the 0.5B to 1.5B difference although the shipped scores would allow a paired bootstrap, and does not engage with the zero-shot detector or calibration literature, so a researcher can use it as a pilot data point, not as evidence about scale. Cheapest fix: one test that runs analyse() on the committed score caches and asserts the headline values (0.2775, 0.3292, 27/32), plus a paired bootstrap line in the README.
